Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-10.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Current neuroscience research relies heavily on functional localizer (fLoc) experiments to identify regions of the cerebral cortex that respond to specific concepts (e.g., faces, places, words). However, this experiment-driven paradigm faces a critical bottleneck: it depends on manually constructed, fixed sets of visual stimuli and expensive, time-consuming fMRI data collection. These manual stimulus sets are often biased, limited in scope, and place objects in unnatural contexts, leading to questions regarding the ecological validity and generalizability of the identified cortical regions. Consequently, our ability to map the brain’s functional organization is severely constrained by the scarcity of real biological data.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that we can overcome data scarcity by moving from a discriminative to a **generative** modeling paradigm. We propose that a generative model, trained on existing fMRI-image pairs, can learn the underlying conditional probability distribution of brain activity in response to visual input. By effectively simulating a "virtual brain," we can synthesize high-fidelity neural responses to an infinite variety of arbitrary visual stimuli. This will allow us to conduct "in silico" functional localization experiments, statistically identifying concept-selective regions for novel categories without requiring physical fMRI scans.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)

We propose a generative encoding framework designed to map arbitrary visual stimuli to synthetic fMRI recordings. The architecture will consist of three distinct logical stages:

**1. Latent Space Projection and Alignment**
Raw fMRI data is inherently noisy and high-dimensional. To manage this, we will implement an **fMRI Autoencoder**.
*   **Encoder:** Projects voxel-level data into a compressed, high-dimensional latent representation.
*   **Alignment:** Crucially, we will align this fMRI latent space with a pre-trained visual semantic space (derived from a large-scale vision model). This ensures that the brain signal representations are semantically consistent with the visual stimuli they represent.

**2. Generative Distribution Modeling**
Unlike traditional regression models that assume a deterministic one-to-one mapping between image and brain activity, we acknowledge that neural responses exhibit variance (one-to-many correspondence).
*   **Diffusion Estimator:** We will utilize a diffusion-based architecture to model the conditional distribution of fMRI latent representations given a visual stimulus.
*   **Mechanism:** The model will learn to reverse a noise process, progressively denoising a random signal conditioned on the semantic features of the input image, eventually yielding a predicted fMRI latent vector.

**3. Inference and Virtual Trials**
To simulate the biological phenomenon of "trials" (repeated exposures to ensure signal stability):
*   **Multi-Trial Synthesis:** We will generate multiple synthetic fMRI outputs for a single image by sampling from the diffusion model multiple times with different noise initializations.
*   **Correlated Noise:** To mimic the intra-subject reproducibility found in biological brains, we will introduce correlated noise during sampling, ensuring the variance resembles natural neural fluctuations. These trials will be averaged to produce a robust final synthetic recording.

**4. Data-Driven Localization Strategy**
Once the model is trained, we will perform localization by:
*   Selecting large sets of unlabelled images containing specific concepts (e.g., "food," "surfer").
*   Synthesizing fMRI responses for these images using the model.
*   Applying statistical tests to the synthetic voxels to identify regions that consistently activate for specific concepts, effectively creating a map of concept-selective regions.

## Expected Contribution
*   **Theoretical:** We aim to demonstrate that generative modeling is superior to regression for brain encoding, as it captures the intrinsic stochasticity and distribution of neural responses rather than just the mean.
*   **Practical:** This approach enables "zero-shot" fMRI experimentation. Researchers will be able to hypothesize and localize fine-grained concept regions (beyond standard categories like faces/places) using massive external image datasets, serving as a powerful hypothesis-generation tool for future neuroscience studies.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We conducted a comprehensive evaluation of the "MindSimulator" generative fMRI encoding model, assessing its ability to synthesize fMRI data and localize brain concept-selective regions.

*   **Datasets:**
    *   **Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD):** Whole-brain fMRI dataset from 8 subjects viewing MSCOCO images.
    *   **Subjects:** We utilized data from Subj01, Subj02, Subj05, and Subj07 (subjects who completed all sessions).
    *   **Training Split:** Approximately 9,000 unique images per subject (3 trials per image).
    *   **Evaluation Split:** Approximately 1,000 shared images (3 repeats averaged).
    *   **Out-of-Distribution (OOD) Datasets:** CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 (10,000 images from test sets) were used to test generalization.
    *   **Stimuli Selection for Localization:** Images selected from MSCOCO using CLIP zero-shot classification for specific concepts (places, bodies, faces, words, surfer, plane, food, bed).

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **Voxel-Level Metrics:** Pearson correlation, Voxel-wise Mean Square Error (MSE), R-squared ($R^2$), Connectivity Graph similarity (Mean Absolute Error), Spatial Gradient difference, fMRI Representation Similarity (two-way classification accuracy).
    *   **Semantic-Level Metrics (Image Reconstruction Quality):**
        *   **Low-level:** PixCorr (Pixel-wise correlation), SSIM (Structural Similarity Index).
        *   **High-level (Perceptual/Semantic):** Two-way identification accuracy using AlexNet (layers 2 and 5), InceptionV3 (last pooling layer), and CLIP (ViT-L/14 final layer).
        *   **Distance Metrics:** Eff (EfficientNet-B1 average correlation distance), SwAV (SwAV-ResNet50 average correlation distance).
    *   **Localization Metrics:** Accuracy and F1-score (comparing predicted regions against empirical fLoc regions).

*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **Linear Regression Model:** Projects image representation to latent space then to voxels.
    *   **Transformer Encoding Model:** Uses ROI queries and cross-attention (Adeli et al., 2023).
    *   **Ground Truth fMRI (Upper Bound):** Performance metrics calculated using the actual recorded fMRI.
    *   **Grad-CAM based localization:** Compared qualitatively for region localization.

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Hardware:** NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPU.
    *   **Image Extractor:** Pre-trained CLIP ViT-L/14 (frozen).
    *   **fMRI Autoencoder:** Trained for 300 epochs, AdamW optimizer, cycle learning rate starting at 3e-4. Latent dimension 256.
    *   **Diffusion Estimator:** 6 Transformer blocks, 100 timesteps ($\tau$), cosine noise schedule, 0.2 condition drop. Trained for 150 epochs.
    *   **Inference:** Synthesis took approximately 300ms per fMRI.
    *   **Decoding Model for Evaluation:** MindEye2 (Scotti et al., 2024b).
    *   **Localization Statistics:** Voxel-wise one-sample t-test with Bonferroni correction; significance threshold set to 0.01.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

*   **Synthesis Fidelity:** We observed that fMRI synthesized by the MindSimulator contained more accurate neural response patterns compared to the linear regression baseline. Reconstructions from synthetic fMRI displayed accurate concepts, colors, backgrounds, and numbers of objects. The semantic differences between seen visual stimuli and reconstructed stimuli from synthetic fMRI were negligible.
*   **Semantic Metrics:** Noise decoding experiments confirmed that random input, shuffled ground truth fMRI, and shuffled synthetic fMRI yield baseline performance (near 50% for classification metrics, near 0 for correlations). This validates that the semantic metrics employed successfully capture visual semantics contained in fMRI.
*   **Multi-Trial Enhancement:** We found that averaging multiple trials improved both MSE and semantic-level metrics. We attributed this to the use of correlated noise, which reduced variance in neural patterns across encoding trials.
*   **OOD Generalization:** When encoding out-of-distribution images (CIFAR-10/100), the synthetic fMRI retained accurate visual semantics. Reconstructed images from these datasets showed minimal decrease in quantitative metrics, and in some cases (e.g., CLIP score on CIFAR-10) showed improvement over MSCOCO.
*   **Data-Driven Localization:**
    *   **Stimuli Distribution:** We noted significant distribution differences between the unnatural/isolated stimuli used in traditional fLoc experiments and the natural scene images selected for our method.
    *   **Region Prediction:** Despite these distribution differences, our method successfully localized places- and bodies-selective regions that overlapped with empirical findings. The MindSimulator outperformed linear regression in localization accuracy and F1 scores.
    *   **Novel Regions:** We successfully localized novel regions for concepts such as "surfer," "plane," "food," and "bed." These regions were predominantly found in the higher visual cortex, with minimal overlap between concepts.
    *   **Disconnected Regions:** Localization often resulted in several disconnected regions, which appeared to stem from concept coupling (e.g., "surfer" coupling with "sea" and "human").
*   **Voxel Ablation Verification:** Masking the localized surfer-selective region resulted in the disappearance of the corresponding concept objects (e.g., the surfer and the sea) in the reconstructed images, validating the localization accuracy.
*   **Inter-subject Consistency:** Activation patterns for the same concepts (surfer, plane, food, bed) were similar across different subjects (Subj01, 02, 05, 07), with the strongest activation areas typically occurring in the same cortical locations.
*   **Comparison with Grad-CAM:** We observed that our method localized concept-selective regions more focused on the higher-level visual cortex compared to Grad-CAM-based localization methods.

Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# ICLR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the LaTeX paper writing process for ICLR 2025.

## General Setup
* **Document Class:** `\documentclass{article}`
* **Required Packages:**
    ```latex
    \usepackage{iclr2025_conference,times}
    \usepackage{hyperref}
    \usepackage{url}
    % Optional but recommended for math
    \input{math_commands.tex}
    ```
* **Style Files:** You must use `iclr2025_conference.sty` and `iclr2025_conference.bst`.

## Anonymity (Crucial)
* ICLR is double-blind. **Do not** include real author names or affiliations in the submission version, use "Ambitious AI Researcher" instead.
* Use the third person when citing your own prior work (e.g., "Earlier work by Smalle (2024)..." instead of "In our earlier work...").
* You may post your paper on arXiv, but do not explicitly refer to the arXiv version in the paper to maintain anonymity.

## Paper Length
* **Main Text:** Strict upper limit of **10 pages**.
* **Citations:** Unlimited additional pages.
* **Ethics & Reproducibility Statements:** Optional. Do not count toward the page limit (max 1 page each).
* **Acknowledgments:** Do not count toward the page limit.

## Abstract
The abstract must be limited to **one paragraph**.
* **Margins:** Indented 1/2 inch (3 picas) on both left and right-hand margins.
* **Font:** 10-point type, vertical spacing of 11-points.
* **Title:** The word `\textsc{Abstract}` must be centered, in small caps, and in point size 12.
* **Spacing:** Two line spaces precede the abstract.

## Formatting Your Paper
The text must be confined within a rectangle 5.5 inches (33 picas) wide and 9 inches (54 picas) long. The left margin is 1.5 inch (9 picas).
* **Font:** Times New Roman (via `times` package) is preferred.
* **Size:** 10-point type with 11-point vertical spacing.
* **Paragraphs:** Separated by 1/2 line space, with **no indentation**.
* **Paper Title:** 17-point, small caps, left-aligned.

### Headings
* **First Level:** Small caps (`\textsc`), flush left, 12-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Second Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Third Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.

## Citations and References
Use the `natbib` package (loaded automatically by the style file).
* **Narrative citation:** Use `\citet{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "Gomu et al. (2024)".
* **Parenthetical citation:** Use `\citep{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "(Gomu et al., 2024)".
* **Bibliography:**
    ```latex
    \bibliography{references}
    \bibliographystyle{iclr2025_conference}
    ```

## Figures and Tables
* All artwork must be neat, clean, and legible.
* **Captions:** Lower case (except for first word and proper nouns).
* **Placement:**
    * **Figures:** Caption appears **after** (below) the figure.
    * **Tables:** Caption appears **before** (above) the table.

### Example Code for Figures
```latex

\begin{center}

\fbox{\rule[-.5cm]{0cm}{4cm} \rule[-.5cm]{4cm}{0cm}}
\end{center}

```

```latex
\label{sample-table}

\\ \hline \\

Axon             &Output terminal \\
Soma             &Cell body (contains cell nucleus) \\
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

```

## Math Notation
* ICLR encourages standardized notation using `\input{math_commands.tex}` (based on the Deep Learning book notation).
* Variables: Italics ($a$, $\va$, $\mA$).
* Random Variables: Roman ($P(\ra)$).
* Sets: Blackboard bold ($\R$, $\sA$).
* Functions: Standard LaTeX ($f(\vx)$).

## Optional Statements
These should appear at the end of the main text, before references.
1.  **Ethics Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Address potential concerns (human subjects, sensitive data, bias, etc.).
2.  **Reproducibility Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Reference code, proofs, or data processing steps to ensure reproducibility.

## Important Rules

references.text:
## Problem Statement
The precise localization of concept-selective regions within the human cerebral cortex is a fundamental goal in neuroscience. Currently, this process relies heavily on "functional localizer" (fLoc) experiments, where subjects undergo Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) while viewing manually constructed sets of visual stimuli. This experiment-driven paradigm suffers from severe limitations:
1.  **Data Scarcity:** Real fMRI data acquisition is prohibitively expensive and slow, restricting localization efforts to a small set of predefined categories.
2.  **Stimulus Bias:** The manual selection of visual stimuli introduces subjective bias and typically relies on isolated objects in unnatural contexts, raising concerns about the ecological validity and generalizability of the identified cortical regions.
3.  **One-to-One Mapping Limitations:** Existing computational approaches primarily use regression models to map images to fMRI activity. These models assume a deterministic one-to-one mapping, failing to account for the stochastic nature of brain activity where the same stimulus can elicit varying neural response patterns across trials.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose **MindSimulator**, a data-driven generative framework designed to synthesize high-fidelity individual fMRI responses corresponding to arbitrary concept-oriented visual stimuli.

Our core hypothesis is that fMRI encoding should be modeled as a conditional generation problem rather than a regression problem. By learning the conditional probability distribution of brain activity given a visual stimulus, we can capture the intrinsic variance and "one-to-many" nature of neural responses. We hypothesize that a Latent Diffusion Model (LDM), aligned with a pre-trained visual semantic space, can generate synthetic fMRI data indistinguishable from real recordings. This will allow for the statistical localization of concept-selective regions using massive amounts of synthetic data, bypassing the physical constraints of traditional fLoc experiments.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

Our framework consists of three integrated modules: an fMRI Autoencoder for latent representation learning, a Diffusion Estimator for conditional distribution modeling, and an Inference Sampler for high-fidelity synthesis.

### 1. fMRI Autoencoder and Cross-Modal Alignment
Directly modeling high-dimensional, low signal-to-noise fMRI voxels is computationally intractable. We will first train an autoencoder to project raw voxels into a compressed, high-dimensional latent space, aligning this space with visual semantics.

Let $x \in \mathbb{R}^l$ denote preprocessed fMRI BOLD voxels and $y$ denote the corresponding visual stimulus (image). We define a voxel encoder $\mathcal{E}(\cdot)$ and a voxel decoder $\mathcal{D}(\cdot)$. The encoder maps voxels to a latent representation $\mathcal{X} = \mathcal{E}(x) \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times d}$, resulting in $md$-dimensional tokens. The decoder reconstructs the voxels $\hat{x} = \mathcal{D}(\mathcal{X})$.

To ensure the latent space captures visual semantics, we will align the fMRI representation $\mathcal{X}$ with the image representation $\mathcal{V}$ derived from a pre-trained CLIP ViT image extractor, denoted as $\mathcal{V} = \mathcal{V}(y) \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times d}$.

We will train the autoencoder end-to-end using a joint objective function consisting of a reconstruction loss and a cross-modal alignment loss.
The reconstruction loss is the Mean Squared Error (MSE):
$$ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mse}} = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim S} { || x - \hat{x} ||_{2}^{2} } $$

For alignment, we will employ a **SoftCLIP loss** with a cosine-scheduled temperature factor $\tau$ to supervise the relationship between the fMRI latent batch $\mathcal{S}$ and the image latent batch:
$$
\begin{array}{rlr} & {} & {\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{softclip}} = -\displaystyle \frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}|} \sum_{i=1}^{|\mathcal{S}|} \sum_{j=1}^{|\mathcal{S}|} \left[ \frac{\exp(\mathcal{X}_{i} \cdot \mathcal{X}_{j} / \tau)}{\sum_{k=1}^{|\mathcal{S}|} \exp(\mathcal{X}_{i} \cdot \mathcal{X}_{k} / \tau)} \cdot \log \left( \frac{\exp(\mathcal{Y}_{i} \cdot \mathcal{X}_{j} / \tau)}{\sum_{k=1}^{|\mathcal{S}|} \exp(\mathcal{Y}_{i} \cdot \mathcal{X}_{k} / \tau)} \right) \right]} \\ & {} & {-\displaystyle \frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}|} \sum_{i=1}^{|\mathcal{S}|} \sum_{j=1}^{|\mathcal{S}|} \left[ \frac{\exp(\mathcal{Y}_{i} \cdot \mathcal{Y}_{j} / \tau)}{\sum_{k=1}^{|\mathcal{S}|} \exp(\mathcal{Y}_{i} \cdot \mathcal{Y}_{k} / \tau)} \cdot \log \left( \frac{\exp(\mathcal{X}_{i} \cdot \mathcal{Y}_{j} / \tau)}{\sum_{k=1}^{|\mathcal{S}|} \exp(\mathcal{X}_{i} \cdot \mathcal{Y}_{k} / \tau)} \right) \right].} \end{array}
$$
The total objective is:
$$ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{autoencoder}} = \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mse}} + \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{softclip}} $$

### 2. Diffusion Estimator
We will implement a diffusion model to learn the conditional probability distribution of the fMRI representation $\mathcal{X}$ given the image representation $\mathcal{V}$. Unlike standard diffusion models that predict noise, our estimator $\mathcal{P}(\cdot)$ will directly predict the target fMRI representation.

We define the forward diffusion process using the reparameterization trick. At timestep $t \sim [1, \dots, T]$, the noised fMRI representation $\mathcal{Z}_{t}^{\mathcal{X}}$ is:
$$ \mathcal{Z}_{t}^{\mathcal{X}} = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}} \cdot \mathcal{X} + \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_{t}} \cdot \epsilon $$
where $\bar{\alpha}_{t}$ is the cumulative noise schedule hyperparameter and $\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ is Gaussian noise.

The diffusion network will be a Transformer architecture that integrates the image condition $\mathcal{V}$ and learnable time embeddings $\mathcal{T}_t$ via cross-attention. The learning objective is to minimize the difference between the predicted and actual fMRI representation:
$$ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{diffusion}} = \mathbb{E}_{\epsilon, t, (x, y) \sim S} [ || \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{t}^{\mathcal{X}}, \mathcal{V}, \mathcal{T}_{t}) - \mathcal{X} ||_{2}^{2} ] $$

### 3. Inference Sampler with Correlated Noise
To generate synthetic data, we reverse the diffusion process:
$$ \hat{\mathcal{Z}}_{t-1}^{\mathcal{X}} = \mathcal{P}(\hat{\mathcal{Z}}_{t}^{\mathcal{X}}, \mathcal{V}, \mathcal{T}_{t}), \quad \hat{\mathcal{Z}}_{T}^{\mathcal{X}} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1), \quad \hat{\mathcal{X}} = \hat{\mathcal{Z}}_{0}^{\mathcal{X}} $$

To mimic the biological consistency of neural responses across repeated trials of the same stimulus, we will implement a **Multi-Trial Enhancement** strategy using **Correlated Gaussian Noise**. Instead of independent noise samples, we will generate $N$ correlated noise vectors to simulate $N$ trials.

We sample two independent noise vectors $\epsilon_1, \epsilon_2 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ and interpolate them using weights $\beta_n$ to create a set of correlated noises $\epsilon_n$:
$$ \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{n} = \sqrt{\beta_{n}} \cdot \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{1} + \sqrt{1 - \beta_{n}} \cdot \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{2}, \quad n \in [1, 2, \cdots, N] $$
We will generate $N$ synthetic fMRI outputs using these correlated noises and average them to obtain the final high-precision synthetic recording.

### 4. Data-Driven Localization Protocol
Using the trained MindSimulator, we will perform concept localization as follows:
1.  **Stimulus Selection:** Use CLIP zero-shot classification to identify natural images from large datasets (e.g., MSCOCO) that strongly align with specific concepts (e.g., "face", "place").
2.  **Synthesis:** Generate synthetic fMRI responses for these thousands of images.
3.  **Statistical Mapping:** Perform voxel-wise t-tests on the synthetic data to identify regions with statistically significant activation, creating a concept-selective cortical map.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Generative Encoding Paradigm:** We will establish the first generative fMRI encoding model that treats neural encoding as a conditional distribution learning problem, offering a theoretical improvement over deterministic regression models by capturing trial-to-trial variability.
2.  **Infinite Data Synthesis:** The framework will enable the generation of massive, high-fidelity fMRI datasets for any visual concept, overcoming the data scarcity bottleneck of physical fMRI scanning.
3.  **Generalized Concept Localization:** We expect to demonstrate that synthetic data can accurately predict empirical concept-selective regions (e.g., FFA, PPA) and, crucially, allow for the discovery of novel concept regions that have never been experimentally mapped due to stimulus limitations.

preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

agent.name: none
agent.how: no external coding agent: EvoScientist's in-process sub-agents (LangChain deepagents)

tools.permissions: think_tool, deepagents built-ins, EvoSkills skills and an execute shell; skill_manager not registered; no search tool

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
